claims.text: The initial material consists of sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are likely a solid solution or amorphous mixture.
The particles are heated in vacuum from 300 K to 1000 K.
Structural evolution during heating is driven by surface-energy minimization and rapid surface diffusion.
Surface-driven kinetics override high-entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion in these nanoparticles.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down below 10 nm because the surface-to-volume ratio is high.
For sub-10 nm particles, the surface term gamma times area dominates the Gibbs free energy.
The mixing enthalpy of Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt is insufficiently negative to maintain a single-phase solid solution against surface-energy effects.
Rapid phase separation and surface segregation will begin below 1000 K, likely above about 500 K.
Au or Pt has the lowest relevant surface energy and will migrate to the particle surface.
Co, Cu, and Ni will segregate into the core or form distinct secondary phases.
Fast nanoparticle surface-diffusion pathways bypass the lattice-distortion and high-activation-energy basis proposed for sluggish bulk diffusion.
The smallest particles disappear through Ostwald ripening, in which material from smaller particles feeds larger particles and reduces total surface area.
Dissolution, evaporation, or direct coalescence may also contribute to the loss of small particles.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will disappear or coalesce into larger particles during heating.
The remaining particles will develop Au/Pt-enriched shells and Co/Cu/Ni-enriched cores or multiphase domains.
The final state will comprise larger segregated particles rather than a stable equiatomic solid solution.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion can stabilize equiatomic multielement solid solutions and are associated with thermal stability in high-entropy alloys.
For bulk material or particles larger than 50 nm, sluggish diffusion and high-entropy stabilization may dominate and preserve a single-phase structure.
Retention of a single-phase equiatomic structure with no segregation and no particle-size change after heating to 1000 K would falsify the proposed surface-driven mechanism.
